strengths: Addresses a clear gap in benchmarking: CMARL is genuinely underexplored and MEAL is the first benchmark tailored for this setting
Thoughtful technical design with comprehensive environment validation (10 rules ensuring solvability) and procedurally generated tasks avoiding overfitting to fixed task sets
JAX-based GPU acceleration is practical, enabling training on longer task sequences than traditional CPU-bound benchmarks

Well-designed evaluation with clearly defined metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity) appropriate for continual learning, including proper ablation study identifying multi-head architectures as critical
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details in appendices, seed-controllable procedural generation, and complete hyperparameter specifications
Comprehensive plasticity degradation analysis (Section 5.6) demonstrating that MEAL exhibits known pathologies from single-agent continual learning
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging scope constraints (fully observable, 2-agent, discrete actions, layout-only task changes)
weaknesses: Extremely narrow domain scope severely limits generalizability: only Overcooked with layout changes; no dynamics variation, partner changes, agent count scaling, partial observability, or competitive settings tested

Disconnect between abstract claims and actual experiments: claims 'sequences of 100 tasks' but main experiments use only 20 tasks; longer sequences critical for continual learning research, making 20 tasks relatively short

Limited novelty and shallow analytical insights: purely empirical/engineering contribution with no new methods proposed; results mostly confirm expected outcome (naive CL+MARL combinations fail) without mechanistic explanation of why inter-agent conventions break down or how to address it

Only tests one MARL algorithm (IPPO): missing comparisons with value decomposition methods (QMIX, VDN), communication-enabled approaches, curriculum learning, or memory-augmented methods despite coordination being central to the problem
Normalization scheme underestimates performance where agents parallelize work—exactly where cooperation matters most; paper acknowledges but doesn't explore implications for result interpretation
Task-incremental learning only: doesn't explore class-incremental, domain-incremental, or other continual learning paradigms, limiting scope further

Questionable experimental findings warrant deeper investigation: task ID having negligible effect (Figure 5) is counterintuitive; CNN catastrophic failure on small grids seems like implementation choice; Level 3 performance (~0.2) suggests methods may not reliably solve harder tasks

GitHub repository URL not provided; some hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (λ values of 10^11, 10^9, 10^7) without sensitivity analysis; wall-clock timing comparisons absent despite acceleration claims

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First benchmark specifically designed for continual multi-agent RL
Practical impact: First end-to-end GPU-accelerated continual RL library enabling efficient training on 100+ task sequences (hours vs. days)
Rigorous experimental evaluation: 6 baselines, 3 difficulty levels, 5 seeds, comprehensive ablations, and honest confidence intervals
Sound technical design: Well-validated procedural generation pipeline with 10 explicit solvability criteria; proper normalization for variable-sized environments
Key insights: Identifies multi-head architectures as critical; demonstrates plasticity loss in multi-agent settings; reveals existing methods fail on complex coordination tasks
Reproducibility: Extensive hyperparameter documentation, implementation details in appendices, clear experimental protocol
Well-executed engineering: Clean integration of JAX/JaxMARL with continual learning metrics; comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited domain scope: Single environment (Overcooked) with only layout variation; no variation in partner agents or environment dynamics; discrete actions only; 2-3 agents maximum; omits real-world complexity (language, negotiation, planning)

Restricted continual learning setting: Task-incremental paradigm with known task identity during training/evaluation more restrictive than class/domain-incremental; layout changes only, not partner or dynamics shifts

Limited algorithmic coverage: Only IPPO/PPO tested as base MARL algorithm; MAPPO underperformance explanation is cursory; no evaluation of value decomposition methods (VDN, QMIX) or recent MARL algorithms
Performance calibration concerns: Level 1 too easy (EWC: 0.839 with 0.031 forgetting), Level 3 too hard (best: 0.306); poorly calibrated difficulty may limit ability to discriminate methods

Limited novelty: Contribution is primarily engineering (integration) rather than algorithmic or theoretical; individual components (Overcooked, procedural generation, JAX, CL metrics) are existing work

Incomplete experimental design: Key findings relegated to appendices (curriculum learning shows 2x improvement, designated roles, PO variants); no isolated comparison of MARL-specific vs. continual learning challenges

Methodological limitations: Normalization upper bound underestimates multi-agent throughput (acknowledged); forward transfer requires expensive single-task baselines; task-identity assumption unrealistic for many applications
Hyperparameter concerns: Extreme λ values (10^11, 10^9, 10^7) for CL methods lack sensitivity analysis; unclear if results robust to these choices
